name: How Safe Does This Street Look? Rio de Janeiro 15-second safety rating
description:
Method replication: same task, scales and design as the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (150 new Google Street View views of Rio de Janeiro, captured 2016–2026, 800×600 px as in the paper, © Google). Based on De La Puente, Sante, Moreno-Vera, Diaz & Poco, "UrbanGazeVis: A Visualization System for Analyzing Eye-Tracking Data on Urban Safety Perception" (Computers & Graphics, 2026; arXiv:2608.21686). Each participant sees 50 of the 150 street views one at a time; the picture stays on screen for 15 seconds before the rating buttons unlock, then perceived safety is rated from 1 (very unsafe) to 10 (very safe). In the paper, 30 students rated 50 images each (three blocks of 10 raters, 1,500 ratings) while a HoloLens 2 recorded their gaze; safety scores were linked to gaze on disorder cues such as damaged walls, graffiti and overhead cables.

Differences from the original study: (1) no eye tracker and no gaze calibration (the original used a HoloLens 2 head-mounted display in a lab); (2) images are random Street View views across Rio, not the paper's 150 images chosen by multivariate stratified sampling; (3) each participant gets a random draw of 50 images instead of a fixed block of 50; (4) the picture stays visible while rating, and there is no 5-second blank between images and no familiarisation with one safe and one unsafe reference image; (5) age group, gender and a familiarity-with-Rio question were added at the end.
author: De La Puente, Sante, Moreno-Vera, Diaz & Poco
